body.text: Former Vice-President (VP) Gibran Rakabuming Raka’s resignation on 12 November, after he came under threat of impeachment, has severed the most visible link between President Prabowo Subianto’s government and his predecessor (and Gibran’s father) Joko Widodo (Jokowi). It came six weeks after Prabowo swore in 44 officials, replaced the police chief and brought religious leaders and critics into a new Presidential Advisory Council (Wantimpres). These events should be analysed together: while Cabinet posts are the President’s prerogative to give or take away, — and he has done so in multiple reshuffles — what is new is that this logic has now reached high offices meant to stand apart from the presidency and, more importantly, balance it. These include the national police, the moral voice and weight of religious leaders and a directly elected VP (Table 1).

The choice of Gibran’s successor, which the Constitution leaves largely to the president, will show how far Prabowo’s power consolidation can go. The president nominates two candidates within 14 days of the VP post going vacant, and the People’s Consultative Assembly (MPR) has 60 days to choose from the two nominees.

Prabowo has been a powerful president since his inauguration in October 2024. First, his large ruling coalition holds 470 of 580 parliamentary (DPR) seats. What his Cabinet reshuffles and Gibran’s exit signify is not how much more power Prabowo holds today, but that the capacity of institutions to correct this power, that is, to scrutinise, question and restrain the president, has been narrowed.
Arguably, Parliament moved against Gibran not as an overseer of presidential power, but as an extension of it.

First, the country’s coercive apparatus: the National Police, the Executive Office of the President (KSP) and the Coordinating Ministry for Politics and Security are now led by figures beholden to the president. The DPR approved the new police chief within a day, two months after denying any such plan while the outgoing chief, a Jokowi loyalist, was moved to the palace as presidential chief of staff.

Second, control over Indonesia’s extractive economy has been formalised in a new Coordinating Ministry for Downstreaming and Energy Transition, which along with the energy ministry, now sits with Golkar, the largest coalition partner. The president handing the new coordinating ministry to Golkar chairman Bahlil Lahadalia, who remains energy minister, deepens what political scientist Dan Slater calls “party cartelisation”: parties trading opposition for access to state resources.

Third, some religious leaders and figures from business, retired generals and even critics who were outside the state apparatus have been co-opted as paid advisers to the president. Each member reportedly receives IDR76.5 million (about USD4,200) a month, a modest price for consolidating support. While such appointments do not guarantee loyalty, and one advisor, Rocky Gerung, vowed to stay critical, acceptance of a Wantimpres position is a signal. For instance, leaders of Nahdlatul Ulama and the Indonesian Ulema Council, now sworn in by the president and paid by the state, are perhaps signaling to their millions of followers that they align with the government.

Fourth, a significant political succession now rests with the president. Arguably, Parliament moved against Gibran not as an overseer of presidential power, but as an extension of it. Now, as per the Constitution, Prabowo will nominate two candidates from which the MPR (dominated by his coalition) elects a new vice-president.

The likely consequence of all this is further democratic erosion in Indonesia through the quiet loss of corrective mechanisms on executive power. This lands on a democracy already in retreat. V-Dem now classifies Indonesia as an “electoral autocracy”; by some polls, Prabowo’s approval fell from 81.2 to 51.1 per cent in eight months. As institutional channels narrow, correction has moved to the street, but police have blocked protests and attacked marchers. There are also signs within the political elite that all is not well. The wiretapping case, where a former police chief and accomplices allegedly tapped the sitting president and other politicians, as well as journalists and NGOs, has been framed by the presidential palace as possible treason. Yet neither the street nor elite infighting is a reliable form of correction for a democracy.

The contest to succeed Gibran shows who now competes for proximity to power. Prabowo has said he will consult coalition parties first. Four camps are in play. Coalition party chiefs, including the Democrats’ Agus Harimurti Yudhoyono, may see the post as a springboard to 2029, but may threaten the president’s electability in time if they are young and popular. Gerindra loyalists, like Deputy Speaker Sufmi Dasco Ahmad and former foreign minister Sugiono, among those named as potential candidates, offer loyalty. DPR Speaker Puan Maharani could bring in her mother’s Indonesian Democratic Party of Struggle (PDI-P), the last large party holdout outside the coalition. Finally, retired generals, whose forum demanded Gibran’s removal as early as April 2025, would welcome one of their own as Prabowo’s new deputy.

Whoever prevails in the VP selection will owe their post to Prabowo rather than to voters. Choosing a person from any of the camps above would remove a different check against the president’s power: a party chief could unsettle coalition bargaining as could a loyalist, Puan could end parliament’s independence, and a former general would test civilian supremacy.

The last scenario deserves attention. A retired general as VP under Prabowo, himself an ex-general, would give Indonesia its first all-military presidential pair since Suharto and Try Sutrisno (1993–98) and crown a drift from civilian rule already visible. Security figures run the president’s staff, security coordination, the police and even the new agrarian reform agency, while a revised law lets officers hold more civilian posts. What more, a deputy drawn from a command culture is unlikely to act as an internal check against his superior.

Sidelined parties may push back in the MPR vote, turning the issue of VP succession into elite bargaining rather than one of public interest — either way, the reform-era post-1998 settlement that took the military out of politics would be hollowed out further. Whoever Prabowo nominates, the real test is whether any institution can still tell him “No”. As things stand, very few can.
